header:
How to invest in
index funds

lines.text: Over 15 years, about 9 in 10 stock-picking funds trailed this.
lines.say: Over fifteen years, about nine in ten stock-picking funds trailed this.

lines.text: That's large-cap funds run by pros, versus the S&P 500, per S&P's SPIVA scorecard through June 2026.
lines.say: That's large-cap funds run by pros, versus the S and P five hundred, per S and P's SPIVA scorecard through June twenty twenty-six.

lines.text: And the thing they trailed doesn't pick stocks at all. It just copies a list.
lines.say: And the thing they trailed doesn't pick stocks at all. It just copies a list.

lines.text: Even in the first half of 2026, a friendlier stretch for stock pickers, 67% still trailed.
lines.say: Even in the first half of twenty twenty-six, a friendlier stretch for stock pickers, sixty-seven percent still trailed.

lines.text: This guide walks through investing in index funds, step by step.
lines.say: This guide walks through investing in index funds, step by step.

lines.text: Plus automating, rebalancing, the scary drops, the common mistakes, and a one-screen checklist.
lines.say: Plus automating, rebalancing, the scary drops, the common mistakes, and a one-screen checklist.

lines.text: No fund picks here and no predictions. This is education, not advice.
lines.say: No fund picks here, and no predictions. This is education, not advice.

lines.text: Chapter 1: What an index fund is
lines.say: Chapter one: what an index fund is.

lines.text: An index is just a list of stocks with rules, kind of like a recipe. An index fund buys everything on the list.
lines.say: An index is just a list of stocks with rules, kind of like a recipe. An index fund buys everything on the list.

lines.text: Nobody is guessing which stocks will win. The fund just tries to match the list, minus a small fee.
lines.say: Nobody is guessing which stocks will win. The fund just tries to match the list, minus a small fee.

lines.text: The most famous list is the S&P 500: 500 big US companies, chosen by a committee.
lines.say: The most famous list is the S and P five hundred: five hundred big US companies, chosen by a committee.

lines.text: Together, they make up roughly 80% of the US stock market's value, according to Morningstar.
lines.say: Together, they make up roughly eighty percent of the US stock market's value, according to Morningstar.

lines.text: The index weights companies by market value, so the biggest ones get the biggest slices of the fund.
lines.say: The index weights companies by market value, so the biggest ones get the biggest slices of the fund.

lines.text: A total stock market index goes wider: thousands of companies, big, medium and small.
lines.say: A total stock market index goes wider: thousands of companies, big, medium, and small.

lines.text: Next question: mutual fund or ETF? Both are just wrappers, and both can hold the exact same index.
lines.say: Next question: mutual fund or E T F? Both are just wrappers, and both can hold the exact same index.

lines.text: A mutual fund is priced once a day, after the market closes. An ETF trades on an exchange all day, like a stock, at a price that can drift slightly from the fund's value.
lines.say: A mutual fund is priced once a day, after the market closes. An E T F trades on an exchange all day, like a stock, at a price that can drift slightly from the fund's value.

lines.text: And index funds have taken over. The Investment Company Institute says index funds held 19% of US long-term fund assets in 2010.
lines.say: And index funds have taken over. The Investment Company Institute says index funds held nineteen percent of US long-term fund assets in twenty ten.

lines.text: By 2015 it was 28%, by 2020 it was 40%, and by the end of 2025 it hit 52%. That's a majority.
lines.say: By twenty fifteen it was twenty-eight percent, by twenty twenty it was forty percent, and by the end of twenty twenty-five it hit fifty-two percent. That's a majority.

lines.text: Chapter 2: Before you invest
lines.say: Chapter two: before you invest.

lines.text: Step one comes before buying anything: making sure a surprise bill won't force a sale.
lines.say: Step one comes before buying anything: making sure a surprise bill won't force a sale.

lines.text: The Fed's 2025 household survey found 63% of adults would cover a $400 emergency with cash or its equivalent.
lines.say: The Fed's twenty twenty-five household survey found sixty-three percent of adults would cover a four hundred dollar emergency with cash or its equivalent.

lines.text: That's why many guides put an emergency fund in savings first. Stocks can be down right when the car breaks.
lines.say: That's why many guides put an emergency fund in savings first. Stocks can be down right when the car breaks.

lines.text: The second check is high-interest debt. The average card rate on accounts paying interest was about 22% in August 2026, per Fed data.
lines.say: The second check is high-interest debt. The average card rate on accounts paying interest was about twenty-two percent in August twenty twenty-six, per Fed data.

lines.text: Paying off a card at 22% works like earning a guaranteed 22% on that money.
lines.say: Paying off a card at twenty-two percent works like earning a guaranteed twenty-two percent on that money.

lines.text: No index fund promises that. Returns bounce around, and some years are negative.
lines.say: No index fund promises that. Returns bounce around, and some years are negative.

lines.text: Money needed within a few years, like a down payment, usually isn't kept in stocks, since a drop may not recover in time.
lines.say: Money needed within a few years, like a down payment, usually isn't kept in stocks, since a drop may not recover in time.

lines.text: Chapter 3: Pick the account
lines.say: Chapter three: pick the account.

lines.text: Step two is the account. The index fund is what you own.
lines.say: Step two is the account. The index fund is what you own.

lines.text: The account is the box it sits in, and the box decides the taxes.
lines.say: The account is the box it sits in, and the box decides the taxes.

lines.text: There are three common boxes, and the first is a workplace plan like a 401(k).
lines.say: There are three common boxes, and the first is a workplace plan like a four oh one K.

lines.text: Many employers match part of what you put in. In a made-up example, 50 cents for every dollar, up to 6% of pay.
lines.say: Many employers match part of what you put in. In a made-up example, fifty cents for every dollar, up to six percent of pay.

lines.text: That match is extra money on top of whatever the fund earns, and many plan menus include a broad index fund.
lines.say: That match is extra money on top of whatever the fund earns, and many plan menus include a broad index fund.

lines.text: For 2026, the IRS lets employees put up to $24,500 into a 401(k), plus $8,000 more at age 50 or older.
lines.say: For twenty twenty-six, the I R S lets employees put up to twenty-four thousand, five hundred dollars into a four oh one K, plus eight thousand dollars more at age fifty or older.

lines.text: The second box is an IRA, which you open yourself at a brokerage or fund company.
lines.say: The second box is an I R A, which you open yourself at a brokerage or fund company.

lines.text: For 2026, the IRA limit is $7,500 a year, and that's across all your IRAs combined.
lines.say: For twenty twenty-six, the I R A limit is seventy-five hundred dollars a year, and that's across all your I R As combined.

lines.text: A traditional IRA may give a tax break now, with taxes when you withdraw. A Roth IRA is taxed up front, and qualified withdrawals later are tax-free.
lines.say: A traditional I R A may give a tax break now, with taxes when you withdraw. A Roth I R A is taxed up front, and qualified withdrawals later are tax-free.

lines.text: For single filers in 2026, Roth contributions phase out between $153,000 and $168,000 of income.
lines.say: For single filers in twenty twenty-six, Roth contributions phase out between one hundred fifty-three thousand and one hundred sixty-eight thousand dollars of income.

lines.text: The IRS updates these limits for 2027, so IRS.gov has the newest numbers.
lines.say: The I R S updates these limits for twenty twenty-seven, so I R S dot gov has the newest numbers.

lines.text: The third box is a regular taxable brokerage account. There's no contribution limit, but no special tax break either.
lines.say: The third box is a regular taxable brokerage account. There's no contribution limit, but no special tax break either.

lines.text: In a taxable account, dividends and gains from selling are generally taxed in the year you get them. That matters for rebalancing.
lines.say: In a taxable account, dividends and gains from selling are generally taxed in the year you get them. That matters for rebalancing.

lines.text: Chapter 4: Open it and pick the fund
lines.say: Chapter four: open it and pick the fund.

lines.text: Step three: open and fund the account. It usually takes a Social Security number, a photo ID, and a bank account to link.
lines.say: Step three: open and fund the account. It usually takes a Social Security number, a photo I D, and a bank account to link.

lines.text: If a brokerage fails, SIPC covers customer securities and cash up to $500,000, with a $250,000 cash limit.
lines.say: If a brokerage fails, SIPC covers customer securities and cash up to five hundred thousand dollars, with a two hundred fifty thousand dollar cash limit.

lines.text: But SIPC doesn't cover losses when the market falls. That risk stays with you.
lines.say: But SIPC doesn't cover losses when the market falls. That risk stays with you.

lines.text: Here's the classic beginner mistake: you move in $5,000, and it just sits there as cash. Depositing isn't investing.
lines.say: Here's the classic beginner mistake: you move in five thousand dollars, and it just sits there as cash. Depositing isn't investing.

lines.text: The money only goes to work once you actually place an order for a fund.
lines.say: The money only goes to work once you actually place an order for a fund.

lines.text: Step four: pick the fund. First, which index does it track: the S&P 500, the total market, international stocks, or bonds.
lines.say: Step four: pick the fund. First, which index does it track: the S and P five hundred, the total market, international stocks, or bonds.

lines.text: Second, the expense ratio: the yearly fee, taken right out of the fund as a percent of your money. You never get a bill.
lines.say: Second, the expense ratio: the yearly fee, taken right out of the fund as a percent of your money. You never get a bill.

lines.text: It sounds tiny. A 1% expense ratio is $10 a year for every $1,000 you hold.
lines.say: It sounds tiny. A one percent expense ratio is ten dollars a year for every thousand dollars you hold.

lines.text: In 2024, the average index stock mutual fund charged 0.05%, versus 0.64% for active stock funds, per ICI.
lines.say: In twenty twenty-four, the average index stock mutual fund charged zero point zero five percent, versus zero point six four percent for active stock funds, according to I C I.

lines.text: Index stock ETFs averaged 0.14%. Those averages are weighted by assets, so plenty of funds charge more.
lines.say: Index stock E T Fs averaged zero point one four percent. Those averages are weighted by assets, so plenty of funds charge more.

lines.text: Third, overlap. Two different S&P 500 funds hold the same 500 companies, so owning both doesn't spread the risk.
lines.say: Third, overlap. Two different S and P five hundred funds hold the same five hundred companies, so owning both doesn't spread the risk.

lines.text: And fourth, mutual fund or ETF, which often depends on the account. Many 401(k) menus don't offer ETFs at all.
lines.say: And fourth, mutual fund or E T F, which often depends on the account. Many four oh one K menus don't offer E T Fs at all.

lines.text: So does a fee gap under one percentage point really matter? Let's test it.
lines.say: So does a fee gap under one percentage point really matter? Let's test it.

lines.text: Here's a made-up example: $10,000 invested at the end of every year for 30 years, earning 7% a year before fees.
lines.say: Here's a made-up example: ten thousand dollars invested at the end of every year for thirty years, earning seven percent a year before fees.

lines.text: That 7% is an assumption to keep the math simple, not a prediction. Real returns jump around.
lines.say: That seven percent is an assumption to keep the math simple, not a prediction. Real returns jump around.

lines.text: The only thing we change is the fee: 0.03%, 0.50%, or 1%.
lines.say: The only thing we change is the fee: zero point zero three percent, half a percent, or one percent.

lines.text: At 0.03%, you net 6.97%, and after 30 years you end up with $939,525.
lines.say: At zero point zero three percent, you net six point nine seven percent, and after thirty years you end up with nine hundred thirty-nine thousand, five hundred twenty-five dollars.

lines.text: At 0.50%, you net 6.5% and end up with $863,749.
lines.say: At half a percent, you net six and a half percent and end up with eight hundred sixty-three thousand, seven hundred forty-nine dollars.

lines.text: At 1%, you net 6% and end up with $790,582.
lines.say: At one percent, you net six percent and end up with seven hundred ninety thousand, five hundred eighty-two dollars.

lines.text: Rounded, that's about $940,000 versus $791,000, from the same $300,000 in deposits.
lines.say: Rounded, that's about nine hundred forty thousand versus seven hundred ninety-one thousand dollars, from the same three hundred thousand dollars in deposits.

lines.text: The cheaper fund comes out ahead, because nothing else changed.
lines.say: The cheaper fund comes out ahead, because nothing else changed.

lines.text: The gap is $148,943, from a fee difference of less than one percentage point.
lines.say: The gap is one hundred forty-eight thousand, nine hundred forty-three dollars, from a fee difference of less than one percentage point.

lines.text: Why so big? The fee comes out every year, and that money never gets to compound.
lines.say: Why so big? The fee comes out every year, and that money never gets to compound.

lines.text: At first, the yearly fee on $10,000 is just $50 at 0.50%, or $100 at 1%. Easy to ignore.
lines.say: At first, the yearly fee on ten thousand dollars is just fifty dollars at half a percent, or a hundred dollars at one percent. Easy to ignore.

lines.text: Chapter 5: Automate, rebalance, hold on
lines.say: Chapter five: automate, rebalance, hold on.

lines.text: Step five: automate it, so a fixed amount gets invested every payday without a fresh decision.
lines.say: Step five: automate it, so a fixed amount gets invested every payday without a fresh decision.

lines.text: A 401(k) does this through payroll. For an IRA or taxable account, many brokerages offer automatic deposits and automatic investing.
lines.say: A four oh one K does this through payroll. For an I R A or taxable account, many brokerages offer automatic deposits and automatic investing.

lines.text: Investing the same amount on a schedule is called dollar-cost averaging. When prices are low, the same dollars buy more shares.
lines.say: Investing the same amount on a schedule is called dollar-cost averaging. When prices are low, the same dollars buy more shares.

lines.text: In a made-up example, $500 buys 10 shares at $50 each, but 20 shares at $25.
lines.say: In a made-up example, five hundred dollars buys ten shares at fifty dollars each, but twenty shares at twenty-five dollars.

lines.text: Step six: rebalance. If you hold a mix, like stocks and bonds, the mix drifts as prices move.
lines.say: Step six: rebalance. If you hold a mix, like stocks and bonds, the mix drifts as prices move.

lines.text: Say a made-up target is 80% stocks and 20% bonds. After a strong year for stocks, it might drift to 85% and 15%.
lines.say: Say a made-up target is eighty percent stocks and twenty percent bonds. After a strong year for stocks, it might drift to eighty-five and fifteen.

lines.text: Rebalancing nudges it back by trimming what grew or sending new money to what lagged.
lines.say: Rebalancing nudges it back by trimming what grew or sending new money to what lagged.

lines.text: In a taxable account, selling can trigger taxes, so some people redirect new money instead. Many check once a year.
lines.say: In a taxable account, selling can trigger taxes, so some people redirect new money instead. Many check once a year.

lines.text: Step seven is the hardest: staying the course. An index fund owns the market, so when the market falls, so does the fund.
lines.say: Step seven is the hardest: staying the course. An index fund owns the market, so when the market falls, so does the fund.

lines.text: In 2008, the S&P 500 lost 37%, including dividends.
lines.say: In two thousand eight, the S and P five hundred lost thirty-seven percent, including dividends.

lines.text: In 2022, it lost about 18%.
lines.say: In twenty twenty-two, it lost about eighteen percent.

lines.text: The index hit a record close in October 2007, then fell about 57% to its low in March 2009.
lines.say: The index hit a record close in October two thousand seven, then fell about fifty-seven percent to its low in March two thousand nine.

lines.text: It didn't close at a new record until March 2013, about five and a half years after the old peak.
lines.say: It didn't close at a new record until March twenty thirteen, about five and a half years after the old peak.

lines.text: Selling near the bottom locked in the loss. Staying in got the recovery, though past recoveries don't promise future ones.
lines.say: Selling near the bottom locked in the loss. Staying in got the recovery, though past recoveries don't promise future ones.

lines.text: And after both of those drops came big years: about 26% in 2009, and about 26% again in 2023.
lines.say: And after both of those drops came big years: about twenty-six percent in two thousand nine, and about twenty-six percent again in twenty twenty-three.

lines.text: Nobody knows when the next drop or the next rebound comes. That's exactly why the plan gets made before the drop.
lines.say: Nobody knows when the next drop or the next rebound comes. That's exactly why the plan gets made before the drop.

lines.text: Chapter 6: Mistakes and checklist
lines.say: Chapter six: mistakes and the checklist.

lines.text: First, the common mistakes. Number one is the cash trap: money deposited but never invested.
lines.say: First, the common mistakes. Number one is the cash trap: money deposited, but never invested.

lines.text: Number two is chasing last year's top fund. S&P's persistence research finds few top funds stay on top.
lines.say: Number two is chasing last year's top fund. S and P's persistence research finds few top funds stay on top.

lines.text: Number three is paying high fees for a fund that mostly tracks the market anyway, or owning three S&P 500 funds and calling that diversified.
lines.say: Number three is paying high fees for a fund that mostly tracks the market anyway, or owning three S and P five hundred funds and calling that diversified.

lines.text: And number four is selling in a panic when the market drops, which turns a paper loss into a real one.
lines.say: And number four is selling in a panic when the market drops, which turns a paper loss into a real one.

lines.text: Now the whole guide on one screen: safety net and debt first, then the account, opening and funding it, and comparing funds by index and fee.
lines.say: Now the whole guide on one screen: safety net and debt first, then the account, opening and funding it, and comparing funds by index and fee.

lines.text: Then the actual buy order, automating, rebalancing on a schedule, and the plan for riding out drops.
lines.say: Then the actual buy order, automating, rebalancing on a schedule, and the plan for riding out drops.

lines.text: Two numbers to remember: a 0.05% average index stock fund fee in 2024, and about 9 in 10 large-cap funds trailing over 15 years.
lines.say: Two numbers to remember: a zero point zero five percent average index stock fund fee in twenty twenty-four, and about nine in ten large-cap funds trailing over fifteen years.

lines.text: The boring part is the whole point: a list, a low fee, and a lot of time.
lines.say: The boring part is the whole point: a list, a low fee, and a lot of time.

lines.say: If this helped, subscribe for more step-by-step money guides. Education, not advice.

post.yt_desc:
About 9 in 10 actively managed large-cap funds trailed the S&P 500 over the 15 years to June 2026, according to S&P Dow Jones Indices' SPIVA scorecard. This step-by-step guide explains what an index fund is (S&P 500 vs total market, mutual fund vs ETF), what comes first (an emergency fund and high-interest debt), the account choices with 2026 limits (401(k) $24,500, IRA $7,500; check IRS.gov for 2027), opening and funding an account, comparing expense ratios, automating, rebalancing and riding out drops like 2008 (-37%) and 2022 (-18%). A hypothetical example shows how a 0.03% vs 1% fee changes $10,000 a year over 30 years at an assumed 7%. No fund picks and no predictions.

CHAPTERS

Sources: S&P Dow Jones Indices SPIVA U.S. Mid-Year 2026 (Sept 2026) and Year-End 2025 scorecards; ICI, Trends in the Expenses and Fees of Funds, 2025 (March 2026); ICI Investment Company Fact Book 2025 and 2026; IRS Notice 2025-67 (Nov 2025) and IRS Roth IRA income limits for 2026; Federal Reserve SHED report (May 2026) and G.19 Consumer Credit (Oct 2026); SIPC; SEC Investor Bulletin on ETFs; Morningstar; S&P 500 total returns via S&P Dow Jones Indices; Reuters/NPR (March 28, 2013).

News and education, not financial advice.
